thread.title: Yext, New York Startup, Soars on Amazon Deal

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Yext, New York Startup, Soars on Amazon Deal
text:
Howard Lerman, CEO of Yext, at the company's offices at 1 Madison Ave. in Manhattan. By Tiernan Ray Updated July 25, 2018 5:22 p.m. ET The entire fifth floor of the elegant old Metropolitan Life Tower on East 23rd Street in Manhattan is devoted to the kind of engineering cubes and common spaces you’d see in a typical Silicon Valley startup.
It is the home of Yext ( YEXT ), a 12-year-old cloud-computing outfit that's following in the footsteps of the big, well-established West Coast cloud ventures such as Salesforce.com ( CRM ) and Workday ( WDAY ).
Yext's software provides the information, organized and cleaned up, behind voice searches such as “Where are there McDonald’s near me?” when you use Apple ’s ( AAPL ) Siri assistant on your iPhone.
The stock, which came public a year ago April, is one of the cloud darlings that have been white hot of late. The shares are up roughly 40% since the IPO and up 60% this year.
Yext got a big bounce Wednesday, closing up $3.72, or 20%, at $22.66, after the company announced this morning that its service will be used by Amazon.com ( AMZN ) in its “ Echo ” appliances.
This particular floor of Silicon Alley real estate is a tool for Yext 's CEO and co-founder Howard Lerman to grow his staff of 1,200. Being in New York means he can avoid competing with Silicon Valley for engineering talent, he notes with a smile. Most of Yext's 200 or so engineers are recent college graduates, the best and the brightest from many East Coast schools.
The friendly snack dispensers of M&Ms and Goldfish are there in the employee cafeteria on the west side of the floor, which has spacious views of Madison Square Park. (The CEO’s office has a less thrilling view of the side street; Lerman says the views “belong to the people.”)
Yext offices. At the same time, Lerman has hired grizzled veterans of cloud computing to provide adult supervision, such as his chief financial officer, Steve Cakebread , and his head of sales, David Rudnitsky, both long-time veterans of cloud-computing titan Salesforce.
To span the divide between millennials and graybeards, Lerman, 38, has adopted the curious look of The Man in Black : black mock-turtleneck, black blazer, black slacks.
Has he always worn a mock-turtleneck?
“Yes,” he says, "even before Jobs,” referring to the late Steve Jobs .
Yext is increasingly signing seven-figure deals with clients such as McDonald’s ( MCD ) and numerous other large clients such as Rite Aid, Volvo, and University Health System. They pay Yext a yearly fee to organize their data—on locations, services provided, phone numbers, etc.—and to then populate that data into services such as Siri and Amazon’s Alexa.
Yext’s application, delivered through a Web browser, is “the internal source of truth” for marketing teams inside those big companies. More than their websites, says Lerman, it is where teams go to update company information and design new “ attributes ,” the data points about a business they want to present to the world via Yext’s service—“the critical structured facts” about the company, as Lerman refers to them.
“ This is the app that they live in ,” he says of marketers.
Yext revenue is on course for what the Street thinks will be $226 million in the January-ending fiscal year. But it still is expected to have deep losses for several years into the future.
Lerman’s is a vision where people move farther and farther away from staring into a screen, instead doing an increasing amount of work by speaking questions or commands to a computer.
In China, for example, most individuals use the social media app WeChat to ask for directions, they don’t type it.
“This,” he says, pantomiming a person frantically typing on their smartphone, "is so unnatural."
"People search with voice differently than they type,” he observes. “If I want to know the nutrition information about a Big Mac, I’ll say it in a natural way, like, ‘How many calories are in a Big Mac?’"
And people ask more precise questions, the kind that must be anticipated by a company or a brand. “If I’m in Hamburg, Germany, and I need to find a pet-friendly hotel, my iPhone may not know which ones fit the bill, but that’s the kind of attribute that our customers highlight."
Lerman, a math and science type, nevertheless shows an affinity for speech and language. In his office, the white board is filled with phrases transliterated from Chinese, which Lerman is learning with the help of a tutor.
Though he has previously picked up what sounds like a very good grasp of German, he confesses that his Chinese tutor occasionally addresses him with the Chinese term for “bad student."
In the grand tradition of many motivated and very bright tech founders, he is not entirely suited to formal instruction.
As an American history major at Duke University, where he received his B.A., “I was bored,” he says.
The old Clock Tower building in Manhattan, home to Yext. Lerman found time as an undergraduate to form his first company, an online site called "just a tip dot com," where students could advise friends on their worst habits. He sold that site for $150,000. There followed a string of other private software companies leading up to Yext.
In the reception area, a digital ticker runs along the top of the wall, an idea Lerman picked up from visiting the Bloomberg offices. The ticker shows inscrutable messages like “longitude/latitude changed,” a reference to some of the client attributes that are being updated. Forty percent of the 32 million collective client attributes regularly roll over. It’s a kind of a fever chart of the intensity of information flow in the business.
By signing up more and more companies such as McDonald’s as clients, and by signing more “publishers” such as Amazon, there is a “ network effect ,” contends Lerman, that makes Yext a more and more pivotal hub between parties. Yext works with 150 publishers, including Apple and Amazon.
He is mindful that over time, the Web, and mobile, and computing in general, will change again, just as it has changed before. Fifteen years ago, before mobile, it was things like Mapquest on a desktop PC.
“Today, it's all about Instagram, and Siri, and Uber, and Snapchat,” he reflects. "A decade from now, the publishers will be different again."
Yext, he believes, will remain an essential partner for these companies.
